author: Paul Haeder
title: Commentary: Spill on Aisle Two and the Deep Fryer is Kaput - NewsBreak
text:
By Paul Haeder ,
21 hours ago Aging is not for the faint of heart may have been a popularized saying of Mae West (1883-1980), but in today’s world of 70 percent of Americans with no substantial retirement funds and a less than admirable Social Security check, this statement is magnified in today’s corporate world of usury.
You have few options in Lincoln County if you’re older than 65, in need of income to keep the lights on and the auto running: grocery clerk, associate, server, or worse, short-term rental and hotel bed stripper, AKA maid.
It matters to no one if you have a few decades of high-quality/high-end work experience, or if you have a few college diplomas. Slim pickings all around.
Here I am, age 69 and ‘washed out’ as a driver for Sweet Homes, notorious for high turnover rates because of poor management and the millionaire owners’ cold-cold hearts.
I attempted to do some work at Kroger’s, AKA, Fred Meyer. I applied for the home goods department, was offered the position after an interview, but the “systems” (computerized) never sent me an offer letter.
I called the regional office, and alas, a phone call later, they offered an apology for the laggard response and an offer to work in the “deli,” since the other position had been filled.
I have tons of prime restaurant experience – French, Greek, Italian and Mexican joints. I’ve catered for big venues. The Kroger group said they fought like hell to get me $16.50 an hour, a dollar more than the starting wage.
The closure of Safeway brought dozens of prospective employees over to FM. Yet this company, Kroger, is continuing its multi-year store closing plan.
This national grocery store chain announced in June 2025 that it would shutter 60 stores in less than two years. They call those closures “underperforming” decisions. Kroger describes the closures at a meeting as a way to shift resources away from struggling locations and into stronger markets.
Dirty corporations know little about the community of place – our town is challenged with affordable grocery stores and might end up becoming a food desert if Kroger closes. It’s a Cincinnati-based chain expanding and contracting at the same time.
The bottom line is profits for shareholders, and Kroger’s footprint in 2026 is increasing new store builds by 30%. These are called large-format marketplace stores, slated for Ohio, Texas, and Indiana. The corporation has spent a few billion by acquiring Giant Eagle.
Fred Meyer is “over hiring,” as one manager stated. Many laid-off Safeway workers have come on board. The problem in the deli is that four-letter word – h-e-l-p, or lack thereof.
That also means more work, more chaotic schedules, and a lack of training are part and parcel to what I experienced there. The ovens are leaky, and the hood fan for three ovens and two deep fryers wasn’t working.
Imagine that -- customers wanting deep-fried items with one attendant handling those orders as well as back-of-the-house chicken prepping.
Imagine sinks leaking on the workplace floor, clogged drains, a fridge too small for mountains of boxed poultry.
This is not sustainable, and the scoop from fellow workers is that the hours are long and the demands are intense. Lack of complete staffing makes more work. Some associates in other departments told me that they did not want to cross train because then more demands would be put upon them without any increase in pay.
This job I applied for was to be part-time – less than 32 hours. Each shift I worked was more than that, with two days off. The equipment and training have been faulty. There is no way putting new employees’ feet to the fire or running them through ‘retail bootcamp’ is conducive to customer service and employee satisfaction.
On a national level, I have heard an author talk about her grocery experience: “Cleanup on Aisle Five: Essential Work, Poverty Wages, and the View from Behind the Supermarket Register” chronicles Ann Larson’s experience working as a cashier during the COVID-19 pandemic at an anonymized major grocery chain in Utah.
She’s been asked: What do you think would need to happen to resolve that tension for retail employees nationwide? Her answer: “Pro-human labor policies like a shorter work week, a predictable schedule, and paid sick and vacation days are a start.”
Just five companies already control over 60% of U.S. grocery sales.
First proposed in 2022, a $24.6 billion merger between Kroger’s and Albertsons would have created the largest supermarket monopoly in the US. And the beneficiaries would have been Cerberus Capital Management, the private equity firm that controls Albertsons.
A private equity windfall would come at the expense of shoppers who are already paying 25% more for groceries than four years ago. Analysts say that grocery mergers contribute to price inflation because stores can increase costs when consumers have nowhere else to shop.
The associates and cooks never benefit from these acquisitions, mergers, and closures. These companies are bloodless, for sure, and while most customers understand the hard work and high demands of cooks, servers and preppers, when staffing is low, managers demand more and more from workers. Vacations are rare. Time off requests are denied.
One fellow at another Fred Meyer stated that he’s been there for 12 years and is at the managerial level. However, if he left for whatever reason, for four years and a few months, none of the managerial experience would be counted if he returned. Meaning, he’d start at the minimum wage as a new inexperienced hire would get.
Bloodless.
“While researching the book, I read the French philosopher Simone Weil’s account of working in an auto factory during the 1930s. She concluded that liberty for working people was a ‘search for the material conditions for clear thinking.’ What surprised me the most about writing about the supermarket was how right she was.” -- Ann Larson
[She’ll be interviewed on my KYAQ show, Finding Fringe.]
Paul Haeder is a novelist, journalist, educator and author of “Wide Open Eyes: Surfacing from Vietnam,” Cirque Press
